blocks.x: Winnipeg commercial owners who financed or refinanced when rates were at historic lows may now be renewing in a different world, which makes any renovations before a commercial mortgage renewal worth planning carefully.

The Bank of Canada's policy rate rose [to 2.50% on October 28, 2026](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/10/fad-press-release-2026-10-28/), its first increase since [July 2023](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/07/fad-press-release-2023-07-12/). That is well above where it sat in [2020](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2020/03/press-release-2020-03-27/) and [2021](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2021/12/fad-press-release-2021-12-08/), and lenders may look closely at older buildings.

Whether you're renewing, refinancing or selling, the building's income and condition can shape the outcome. Here's how targeted [commercial building renovations in Winnipeg](/services/commercial-renovations) can strengthen your position, and when to do them.
Why condition matters at renewal or sale
Lenders and buyers usually look at three things:
**Net operating income:** rent collected minus operating costs.
**Occupancy and lease terms:** how much space is leased, and for how long.
**Physical condition:** deferred maintenance can become a deduction from value, or a lender requirement.
Renovations that help lease vacant space, lower operating costs or clear deferred maintenance can help on these fronts.

Timing: start 12 to 18 months ahead
Leasing new space takes time: design, permits, construction, then marketing. To show stronger income at renewal or sale, start well before the date.

**18 months out:** review leases, vacancies and building condition, and ask your lender what it will want to see. Get a building condition assessment if you don't have a recent one, since [some lenders ask for one](https://www.mcap.com/Content/MCAP/Docs/MCAP%20Commercial%20Mortgage%20Document%20Checklist_EN.pdf).
**12 months out:** aim to have vacant-unit renovations, common-area upgrades and envelope repairs done.
**6 months out:** lease up, document improvements, and gather invoices and any manufacturers' warranties for lenders or buyers.
What lenders and buyers may want to see
Invoices and any manufacturers' warranties for recent capital work
Permits closed with final inspections
A list of completed and planned capital improvements
Signed leases for newly renovated space
Consider your buyer

If you're selling, think about who's likely to buy. Owner-occupiers may want move-in-ready space. Investors want leased income and low deferred maintenance. Developers may care more about land and zoning than finishes, so heavy renovation may not pay.
The bottom line
Owners who start early, fix what lenders and buyers are likely to question, and use renovations to lease space before the deadline put themselves in a stronger position for a renewal or sale.
